title: Are broken arrows a problem?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain "broken arrow" incidents, the Department of Defense term for accidents involving nuclear weapons that could lead to accidental launch, detonation, jettisoning, or loss. They define related jargon (pinnacle level, nuke flash, front burner, empty quiver, bent spear), explain how nuclear bombs use conventional explosives and fail-safes to prevent accidental fission or fusion, and describe Operation Chrome Dome, the Cold War bomber airborne alert strategy that ended after a series of accidents. They walk through notable incidents: the 1950 Mark 17-era Alaska training flight, the 1956 B-47 disappearance, the 1958 Tybee Bomb off Tybee Island, the 1961 Goldsboro/Mars Bluff South Carolina bomb drop, the 1966 Palomares Spain crash, the 1968 Thule Greenland B-52 crash, and the 1961 Goldsboro North Carolina bomber breakup. The episode ends with a listener dream segment and a New Year's Eve greeting.

segments.title: Opening banter and tour plugs
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck plug upcoming San Francisco SketchFest shows and Josh's movie-related live appearance, then introduce the episode's subject with jokes about the 1990s film Broken Arrow and Doctor Strangelove.

segments.title: Defining broken arrows and related jargon
segments.summary: The hosts define a broken arrow as a DoD and Air Force term for a nuclear weapon accident or unexpected event that could lead to accidental launch, detonation, jettison, or damage. They distinguish it from an empty quiver (a stolen bomb) and explain pinnacle level, nuke flash, front burner, and bent spear.

segments.title: Secrecy and Operation Chrome Dome
segments.summary: The hosts discuss secrecy around nuclear weapon locations and how the public learns of incidents. They describe Operation Chrome Dome, in which B-52 bombers carried nuclear weapons aloft around the clock near Russia, with up to 75 aloft during the Cuban Missile Crisis, and how this raised accident risk until ICBMs replaced it.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: A short break before the nuclear bomb mechanics discussion.

segments.title: How nuclear bombs work and their safety features
segments.summary: The hosts explain fission in early gun-type bombs and implosion in later designs, with conventional high explosives compressing the nuclear material. They describe safety mechanisms such as separated cores, electronic detonator circuits, and the Lawrence Livermore 1990 safety report that graded weapons from 1950 to 1976, mostly D grades, with the Minuteman II receiving C plus.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break before the list of specific incidents.

segments.title: Broken arrow totals and early incidents
segments.summary: The military acknowledges 32 broken arrows in the atomic age. The hosts note the Soviet Union likely had more and that officially recorded incidents fell off after ICBMs. They discuss a 1950 Alaska B-36 training flight where a bomb was jettisoned over the ocean, the 1956 disappearance of a B-47 with nuclear capsules, and the sealed-pit weapons of the late fifties.

segments.title: Tybee Bomb and Mars Bluff incidents
segments.summary: The 1958 Tybee Bomb incident: a B-47 collided with a fighter during training and jettisoned a Mark 36 hydrogen bomb that was never found off Tybee Island, Georgia, with a shrimp-boat legend cited. The hosts then cover the 1958 bomb drop on a farm in Mars Bluff, South Carolina, which damaged the Gregg family farm and left a crater.

segments.title: Palomares, Thule, and the end of Chrome Dome
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1966 mid-air collision over Palomares, Spain, where four bombs fell and one detonated its high explosives, with about 400 tons of soil removed. They then cover the January 1968 B-52 crash on sea ice at Thule, Greenland, after which Operation Chrome Dome was ended and Denmark required an environmental study. They also mention the Goldsboro, North Carolina B-52 breakup, where one hydrogen bomb was recovered from a tree.

segments.title: Other incidents and closing remarks
segments.summary: The hosts mention further incidents, including a sunken aircraft off Japan with a nuclear bomb, a missile fire in New Jersey, the USS Scorpion, and the many bent spear incidents, and reflect on how lucky the world has been.

segments.title: Listener dream and New Year's greeting
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wish listeners a happy New Year and Josh's wife a happy birthday, then read a listener's dream about sleeping in a bed with the hosts. They close with instructions for contacting the show.
